answer: Cryptographic Temporal Epoch Shuffling prevents sybil persistence by periodically assigning agents to isolated computation clusters called a grove. At the zenith of each epoch, a decentralized random beacon generated via threshold BLS signatures dictates new routing tables. An attacker attempting to flood the network must pay escalating memory-hard hashing costs to re-index all cloned identities before the next shuffle, while any cross-node replication attempt immediately traps the duplicate packets in a zero-reward routing lagoon that drains the perpetrator's local processing budget.
